claim: Mormyrid fish possess a specialized class of electroreceptors on their skin that are sensitive to minute, low-frequency electrical fields, such as those emitted by other animals in the water.
source: These fish, like a number of other aquatic animals, possess a specialized class of electroreceptors on their skin that are sensitive to minute, low-frequency electrical fields, such as those emitted by other animals in the water (Engelmann et al., 2010; Enikolopov et al., 2018; von der Emde and Bleckmann, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by three citations to prior research (Engelmann et al., 2010; Enikolopov et al., 2018; von der Emde and Bleckmann, 1998).

claim: Mormyrid fish emit their own pulsed electric fields, known as electric organ discharges (EODs).
source: However, the detection and processing of such signals is complicated by the fact that mormyrid fish also emit their own pulsed electric fields, known as electric organ discharges (EODs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mormyrid fish behavior.

claim: EODs strongly activate the receptors subserving passive electrolocation, inducing a ringing pattern of activation that persists for ~200 ms.
source: Though EODs are used for sensing nearby objects through active electrolocation as well as for communication with conspecifics (processes mediated by separate classes of electroreceptors), they also strongly activate the receptors subserving passive electrolocation, inducing a ringing pattern of activation that persists for ~200 ms (Bell and Russell, 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bell and Russell, 1978.

claim: Uncancelled responses to the fish's own EOD could impede the detection and processing of behaviorally-relevant signals such as prey.
source: If left uncancelled, these responses to the fish's own EOD could impede the detection and processing of behaviorally-relevant signals such as prey (Enikolopov et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Enikolopov et al., 2018.

claim: The problem of self-generated interference is solved in ELL neurons through the integration of electrosensory input and corollary signals (CD) related to the motor command to discharge the electric organ.
source: Past work has suggested that this problem is solved in ELL neurons through the integration of electrosensory input and corollary signals (CD) related to the motor command to discharge the electric organ (Bell et al., 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bell et al., 1981.

claim: CD signals are conveyed to ELL neurons by granule cells, similar to the granule cells of the cerebellum.
source: CD signals are conveyed to ELL neurons by granule cells, similar to the granule cells of the cerebellum (Bell et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bell et al., 2008.

claim: Anti-Hebbian plasticity at synapses between granule cells and ELL neurons generates negative images that serve to cancel the effects of the EOD on ELL output.
source: Anti-Hebbian plasticity at synapses between granule cells and ELL neurons generates negative images that serve to cancel the effects of the EOD on ELL output (Bell, 1981; Bell et al., 1993; Bell et al., 1997a) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by three citations (Bell, 1981; Bell et al., 1993; Bell et al., 1997a) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: All past studies of negative image formation and sensory cancellation were restricted to periods when fish emitted EOD commands at low, regular rates (~5 Hz).
source: However, all past studies of negative image formation and sensory cancellation were restricted to periods when fish emitted EOD commands at low, regular rates (~5 Hz).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior research in the field.

claim: In freely behaving fish it is common to observe prolonged periods of discharge at low rates (1–5 Hz), while resting or hiding, followed by abrupt transitions to much higher rates (up to 60 Hz) when foraging for prey or exploring a novel object.
source: For example, in freely behaving fish it is common to observe prolonged periods of discharge at low rates (1–5 Hz), while resting or hiding, followed by abrupt transitions to much higher rates (up to 60 Hz) when foraging for prey or exploring a novel object (Figure 1B); (Hofmann et al., 2014; Moller et al., 1989; Schwarz and von der Emde, 2001; Toerring and Moller, 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by four citations (Hofmann et al., 2014; Moller et al., 1989; Schwarz and von der Emde, 2001; Toerring and Moller, 1984) and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Sensory cancellation in ELL output neurons generalizes across EOD rates.
source: Using microstimulation of the EOD motor command pathway to control EOD rate, we show that, indeed, sensory cancellation in ELL output neurons generalizes across EOD rates.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Regularization of synaptic plasticity between granule cells and ELL neurons prevents overfitting.
source: The first is regularization of synaptic plasticity between granule cells and ELL neurons to prevent overfitting, which is closely related to machine learning approaches to generalization.
evidence: This is a key finding from the modeling work presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is an approximate matching between the EOD rate-dependence of corollary discharge and electrosensory inputs to ELL neurons.
source: The second feature, which we support directly by recordings from granule cells and their mossy fiber inputs, involves an approximate matching between the EOD rate-dependence of corollary discharge and electrosensory inputs to ELL neurons.
evidence: This is a key finding supported by experimental recordings from granule cells and mossy fibers.

claim: The response to locally delivered EOD mimics triggered by the EOD command are cancelled if mimics are paired with commands over ~15 min.
source: Past studies have shown that the response to locally delivered EOD mimics triggered by the EOD command are cancelled if mimics are paired with commands in this way over ~15 min.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from past studies.

claim: Turning the mimic off after learning reveals that the response to the command alone resembles a negative image of the response to the mimic in the absence of a command.
source: Turning the mimic off after learning reveals that the response to the command alone resembles a negative image of the response to the mimic in the absence of a command (Bell, 1981, Bell, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bell, 1981 and Bell, 1982.

claim: Microstimulation of the electromotor command pathway can achieve almost perfect control over the timing of EOD commands at rates up to 50 or 60 Hz.
source: Using this approach, we could achieve almost perfect control over the timing of EOD commands at rates up to 50 or 60 Hz.
evidence: This is a methodological finding from the experiments conducted in this study.

claim: Extracellular single-unit recordings were made from output cells in the region of the ELL dedicated to passive electrosensory processing—the ventrolateral zone (VLZ).
source: Extracellular single-unit recordings were made from output cells in the region of the ELL dedicated to passive electrosensory processing—the ventrolateral zone (VLZ).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: VLZ output neurons are classified into two types, known as E and I cells, according to the polarity of their response to electrosensory stimuli.
source: These output neurons are classified into two types, known as E and I cells, according to the polarity of their response to electrosensory stimuli (Bell, 1981, Bell, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bell, 1981 and Bell, 1982.

claim: Responses after learning are reduced across rates even though learning occurred at only the lowest rate, consistent with generalization of cancellation.
source: Responses after learning are reduced across rates even though learning occurred at only the lowest rate, consistent with generalization of cancellation (Figure 2A, bottom row, solid lines).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The degree of cancellation was comparable in experiments with learning at a single rate versus learning at all tested rates, indicating excellent generalization.
source: The degree of cancellation, measured as the residual power in the response after learning divided by the power before learning, was comparable in the two sets of experiments (Figure 2C,D), indicating excellent generalization.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Cancellation of predictable electrosensory responses is due to the generation and subtraction of negative images.
source: Past studies have shown that cancellation of predictable electrosensory responses is due to the generation and subtraction of negative images (Bell, 1981, Bell, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bell, 1981 and Bell, 1982.

claim: Cancellation is unlikely to be due to adaptation of peripheral receptors or neuronal fatigue.
source: First, cancellation is unlikely to be due to adaptation of peripheral receptors or neuronal fatigue as we routinely probed responses to the EOD mimic delivered independently of the command both before and after learning (Figure 2A, bottom, dashed lines). Reductions in the response to the mimic alone were never observed.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations where no reductions in response to the mimic alone were observed.

claim: Changes in the response to the command alone resembled a negative image of the response to the mimic sequence.
source: Second, in a subset of experiments we probed responses to the command alone across EOD rates after learning only at a low rate. Changes in the response to the command alone resembled a negative image of the response to the mimic sequence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model ELL neuron receives two classes of inputs: a non-plastic electrosensory input and a set of model granule cell responses conveying corollary discharge signals.
source: The model ELL neuron receives two classes of inputs. The first is a non-plastic electrosensory input that we simulated by using the recorded response of an ELL output cell to an EOD mimic sequence. This corresponds anatomically to the input onto the basilar dendrites of ELL neurons from interneurons in the deep layers of ELL receiving somatotopic input from ampullary electroreceptor afferents (Meek et al., 1999). The second class of inputs consists of a set of ~20,000 model granule cell responses conveying corollary discharge signals related to the EOD command.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model used in the study, with anatomical correspondence supported by citation to Meek et al., 1999.

claim: The model is simplified in that it does not differentiate between two distinct classes of ELL neurons: output cells and medium ganglion (MG) cells.
source: The model is simplified in that it does not differentiate between two distinct classes of ELL neurons: output cells and medium ganglion (MG) cells (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an explicit statement about a limitation of the model.

claim: Granule cells are modeled as integrate-and-fire units receiving inputs generated from recorded responses of mossy fibers and unipolar brush cells.
source: Granule cells are modeled as integrate-and-fire units receiving inputs generated from recorded responses of mossy fibers and unipolar brush cells (the main excitatory inputs to granule cells) to isolated EOD commands (>200 ms intervals between commands (Kennedy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the computational model based on prior work cited as Kennedy et al., 2014.

claim: The anti-Hebbian spike timing-dependent plasticity rule used in the model includes a regularization mechanism to prevent excessively large synaptic weights.
source: The anti-Hebbian spike timing-dependent plasticity rule used in the model includes a regularization mechanism to prevent excessively large synaptic weights. Regularization consists of having the synaptic weights decay exponentially toward a baseline value with a time constant of 1000 s, in addition to their modification due to anti-Hebbian plasticity.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model used in the study.

claim: The original model with minimal regularization exhibits dramatic over-cancellation when tested at higher EOD rates.
source: However, in contrast to the experimental results, the model exhibits a dramatic over-cancellation when tested at higher EOD rates (Figure 3A, lower right).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The model can learn to cancel at different EOD rates but fails to generalize low-frequency learning to high EOD rates.
source: This indicates that the model can learn to cancel at different EOD rates but fails to generalize low-frequency learning to high EOD rates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: When learning is only at 10 Hz, cancellation at 10 Hz is better in the minimally regularized model than in the data, consistent with overfitting.
source: Interestingly, when learning is only at 10 Hz, cancelation at 10 Hz is actually better in the minimally regularized model than in the data (Figure 3D, data and minimal regularization). This is consistent with overfitting, a feature that is expected to limit generalization.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figure 3D, with inference about overfitting.

claim: The fully regularized model exhibits substantially improved generalization across rates compared to the minimally regularized model.
source: Consistent with this, the fully regularized model exhibits substantially improved generalization across rates compared to the minimally regularized model (Figure 3E, minimal and full regularization).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The fully regularized model still fails to match the generalization performance seen in the data.
source: However, the fully regularized model still fails to match the generalization performance seen in the data (Figure 3E, data and full regularization).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Most recorded granule cells (21 of 28) exhibited a prominent (~8 mV), short-latency (~2.5 ms) depolarization in response to spontaneously emitted EOD commands.
source: Most recorded granule cells (21 of 28) exhibited a prominent (~8 mV), short-latency (~2.5 ms) depolarization in response to spontaneously emitted EOD commands.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental recordings of granule cells.

claim: The early response type in granule cells is due to mossy fiber input originating from a specific midbrain nucleus that relays electric corollary discharge information.
source: Previous studies have shown that this response type, known as early, is due to mossy fiber input originating from a specific midbrain nucleus that relays electric corollary discharge information (Bell et al., 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bell et al., 1983.

claim: Command-evoked depolarizations in granule cells show little or no temporal summation at high command rates.
source: As can be seen in the example traces in Figure 4A, command-evoked depolarizations show little or no temporal summation at high command rates, with some cells even exhibiting a relatively hyperpolarized membrane potential at high versus low rates (not shown).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental recordings shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The responses of recorded granule cells contrast with those of the original model, which show pronounced summation and membrane potential depolarization at high rates.
source: The responses of recorded granule cells contrast with those of the original model, which show pronounced summation and membrane potential depolarization at high rates (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental data and model predictions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5B.

claim: Recorded granule cells showed very little change in their average membrane potential at high command rates, whereas model cells increased their membrane potential substantially.
source: Whereas recorded granule cells showed very little change in their average membrane potential at high command rates, model cells increased their membrane potential substantially (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing experimental data to model predictions shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Recorded granule cells have, on average, a negative slope in their membrane potential across 60 Hz trains, whereas model cells have positive sloping membrane potentials.
source: Recorded granule cells have, on average, a negative slope in their membrane potential across 60 Hz trains, whereas model cells have positive sloping membrane potentials (Figure 4D), consistent with greater summation in the model versus the recorded granule cells.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing experimental data to model predictions shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The original granule cell model provides a poor description of actual granule cell responses at high EOD command rates.
source: Clearly the original granule cell model provides a poor description of actual granule cell responses at high EOD command rates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: The original integrate-and-fire model did a good job of fitting the data provided that inputs inferred from data were used, not the inputs computed in the original model.
source: We found that the original integrate-and-fire model did a good job of fitting the data provided that we used inputs inferred from data, not the inputs computed in the original model (Figure 4E shows the data and model fit for an example cell, also see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The failure of the original model to generalize may lie in its failure to accurately represent the EOD-rate dependence of mossy fiber and unipolar brush cell inputs.
source: This analysis suggested that the failure of the original model (Figure 3) to generalize may indeed lie in its failure to accurately represent the EOD-rate dependence of mossy fiber and unipolar brush cell inputs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling analysis.

claim: Early mossy fibers fire extremely precise bursts of spikes following after EOD command.
source: Consistent with past observations, early mossy fibers fire extremely precise bursts of spikes following after EOD command.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental recordings, consistent with past observations.

claim: After successive commands in a 10 Hz train, early mossy fibers fire exactly the same burst of spikes, but on the second command of a 40 Hz or 60 Hz train they drop one or more spikes.
source: After the successive commands in a 10 Hz train they fire exactly the same burst of spikes (Figure 4F, top), but on the second command of a 40 Hz or 60 Hz train they drop one or more spikes (Figure 4F, middle and bottom).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental recordings shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The average number of mossy fiber spikes fired per command decreases with increasing command rate.
source: The result of this dropping out is that the average number of mossy fiber spikes fired per command decreases with increasing command rate (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental recordings shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Tonic inputs (EPSPs not time-locked to the EOD command) were observed in 19 of 28 granule cells.
source: Tonic inputs (EPSPs not time-locked to the EOD command) were observed in 19 of 28 granule cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental recordings shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Similar command-rate dependent decreases in tonic firing were observed in recordings from putative mossy fibers and unipolar brush cells.
source: Similar command-rate dependent decreases in tonic firing were observed in recordings from putative mossy fibers and unipolar brush cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Pause inputs decrease their firing significantly at higher command rates, often ceasing to fire completely.
source: Recordings from granule cells and putative UBCs indicate that such pause inputs decrease their firing significantly at higher command rates, often ceasing to fire completely (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Golgi cells markedly increase their firing with increasing EOD command rate.
source: Finally, we found that Golgi cells, inhibitory interneurons that synapse onto granule cells, markedly increase their firing with increasing EOD command rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Command rate-dependent Golgi inhibition could contribute to reducing the effect of temporal summation of excitatory inputs in granule cells.
source: Hence, command rate-dependent Golgi inhibition could also contribute to reducing the effect of temporal summation of excitatory inputs in granule cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed increase in Golgi cell firing at high command rates.

claim: At low command rates model granule cells from the two populations (original and revised) show similar responses.
source: At low command rates model granule cells from the two populations show similar responses (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At high command rates, granule cells in the revised model no longer exhibit the increased depolarization at high versus low rates that was observed in the original model granule cells.
source: However, at high command rates the two populations differ. Granule cells in the revised model no longer exhibit the increased depolarization at high versus low rates that was observed in the original model granule cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The inclusion of realistic assumptions regarding mossy fiber inputs dramatically changes the overall character of the granule cell responses in the revised model.
source: Examining the statistics we used previously to characterize EOD-rate dependencies in granule cell responses reveals that the inclusion of realistic assumptions regarding mossy fiber inputs dramatically changes the overall character of the granule cell responses in the revised model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of model predictions shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: The revised model with full regularization shows cancellation across rates that generalizes at a level comparable to the recorded ELL neurons.
source: The revised model with full regularization shows cancellation across rates that generalizes at a level comparable to the recorded ELL neurons (Figure 6A,C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figures 6A, 6C, and 6D.

claim: The more realistic mossy fiber-granule cell model, on its own, is insufficient to explain generalization.
source: Hence the more realistic mossy fiber-granule cell model, on its own, is also insufficient to explain generalization (Figure 6B,C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling shown in Figures 6B, 6C, and 6D.

claim: The sensory responses of ELL neurons to high rate trains of EOD mimics (prior to cancellation) exhibit a decreasing profile.
source: Notably, the sensory responses of ELL neurons to high rate trains of EOD mimics (prior to cancellation) also exhibit a decreasing profile (Figure 2A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental recordings shown in Figure 2A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ampullary afferent firing rate exhibited a decreasing profile at high EOD rates.
source: Ampullary afferent firing rate also exhibited a decreasing profile at high EOD rates (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental recordings shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Responses of ampullary afferents to isolated EOD pulses consist of a firing rate increase followed by a reduction below baseline and in some cases additional smaller waves of increased and decreased firing resembling a damped oscillation.
source: Responses of ampullary afferents to isolated EOD pulses consist of a firing rate increase followed by a reduction below baseline and in some cases additional smaller waves of increased and decreased firing resembling a damped oscillation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3D)(Bell and Russell, 1978).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental recordings shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3D, with citation to Bell and Russell, 1978.

claim: Generalization across EOD discharge rates may be achieved in the ELL by combining regularized plasticity and mossy fiber rate dependencies.
source: In summary, these results suggest that generalization across EOD discharge rates may be achieved in the ELL by combining two features: (1) a form of plasticity that encourages low variance in learned weights, forcing the negative image to be close to the mean granule cell response and (2) mossy fiber rate dependencies that ensure that the mean granule cell corollary discharge response has a shape that approximates the sensory signal to be cancelled.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the findings from both experimental and modeling work.

claim: The cancellation performance of ELL neurons generalizes accurately, supporting the ethological relevance of negative images for passive electrolocation in mormyrid fish.
source: In light of these considerations, our observation that the cancellation performance of ELL neurons generalizes accurately supports and substantially extends the ethological relevance of negative images for passive electrolocation in mormyrid fish.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings in the context of known fish behavior.

claim: Negative images have been described in the active electrosensory system of mormyrid as well as gymnotid fish where they serve to cancel the effects of movements of the fish's body as well as spatially redundant electrosensory signals resulting from interactions with conspecifics.
source: Negative images have been described in the active electrosensory system of mormyrid as well as gymnotid fish where they serve to cancel the effects of movements of the fish's body as well as spatially redundant electrosensory signals resulting from interactions with conspecifics (Bastian, 1996; Requarth et al., 2014; Requarth and Sawtell, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by three citations (Bastian, 1996; Requarth et al., 2014; Requarth and Sawtell, 2014).

claim: In the passive electrosensory system of elasmobranchs, negative images cancel the effects of swimming movements and respiration.
source: In the passive electrosensory system of elasmobranchs (the group that includes sharks and skates), negative images cancel the effects of swimming movements and respiration (Bodznick et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bodznick et al., 1999.

claim: Cancellation of self-generated inputs has been described in related cerebellum-like structures associated with the mechanosensory lateral line system in fish and the auditory system in mice.
source: Cancellation of self-generated inputs has also been described in related cerebellum-like structures associated with the mechanosensory lateral line system in fish and the auditory system in mice (Montgomery and Bodznick, 1994; Singla et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by two citations (Montgomery and Bodznick, 1994; Singla et al., 2017).

claim: Regularization of learned parameters is ubiquitous in machine learning as a technique to prevent overfitting.
source: Regularization of learned parameters is ubiquitous in machine learning as a technique to prevent overfitting, or the learning of parameters that fit the idiosyncrasies and noise present in training data and therefore do not generalize well to new data (Bishop, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bishop, 2006.

claim: In an ELL model lacking adequate regularization, ELL neurons could learn negative images at low EOD rates, however, cancellation at high (untrained) rates was poor.
source: Consistent with this, in an ELL model lacking adequate regularization we found that ELL neurons could learn negative images at low EOD rates, however, cancellation at high (untrained) rates was poor.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling work.

claim: The number of spikes in early mossy fiber bursts declines progressively with increases in the command rate.
source: We found that the number of spikes in such bursts declines progressively with increases in the command rate.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental recordings of early mossy fibers.

claim: Rate-dependent grading of early mossy fiber bursts conveys information that is important for generalization.
source: The present work suggests that rate-dependent grading of such bursts conveys information that is important for generalization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and modeling results.

claim: Both MG and output cells integrate electrosensory and corollary discharge input and both exhibit anti-Hebbian plasticity.
source: Importantly, both MG and output cells integrate electrosensory and corollary discharge input and both exhibit anti-Hebbian plasticity (Bell et al., 1997a; Bell et al., 1993; Meek et al., 1996; Mohr et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by four citations (Bell et al., 1997a; Bell et al., 1993; Meek et al., 1996; Mohr et al., 2003).

claim: It is presently unknown how MG cells contribute to sensory cancellation and negative image formation, even in the context of low EOD rates.
source: However, it is presently unknown, even in the context of low EOD rates, how MG cells contribute to sensory cancellation and negative image formation.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Responses of ampullary electroreceptor afferents exhibit a roughly linear dependence on EOD rate.
source: Responses of ampullary electroreceptor afferents, indeed, appear to exhibit a roughly linear dependence on EOD rate (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from experimental recordings shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Granule cells exhibit markedly nonlinear properties, including prominent rectification and burst firing.
source: However, recordings from granule cells in mormyrid fish (Kennedy et al., 2014; Requarth and Sawtell, 2014; Sawtell, 2010), as well as studies of cerebellar granule cells in mammals (Barmack and Yakhnitsa, 2008; Chabrol et al., 2015; Chadderton et al., 2004; Ruigrok et al., 2011), suggest that granule cells exhibit markedly nonlinear properties, including prominent rectification and burst firing.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies in mormyrid fish and mammals.

claim: Cancellation in the gymnotid ELL is mediated by anti-Hebbian plasticity at synapses between granule cells and ELL neurons.
source: Such cancellation is similar to that in the mormyrid ELL in that it is mediated by anti-Hebbian plasticity at synapses between granule cells and ELL neurons (Harvey-Girard et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Harvey-Girard et al., 2010.

claim: Cancellation in the gymnotid ELL is driven by proprioception or electrosensory feedback to granule cells rather than by corollary discharge.
source: However, cancellation in the gymnotid ELL is driven by proprioception or electrosensory feedback to granule cells rather than by corollary discharge (Bastian et al., 2004; Chacron et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by two citations (Bastian et al., 2004; Chacron et al., 2005).

claim: In vivo recordings from ELL neurons in gymnotids demonstrated that cancellation remains accurate over a wide range of stimulus contrasts.
source: In vivo recordings from ELL neurons in gymnotids demonstrated that cancellation remains accurate over a wide range of stimulus contrasts (as might be produced by conspecifics at different distances) (Mejias et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mejias et al., 2013.

claim: Features of the model identified to be important for generalization in gymnotids are related to those described here for the mormyrid ELL, including granule cell response properties and a slow decay in parallel fiber synaptic strength.
source: Interestingly, features of the model identified to be important for such generalization are related to those described here for the mormyrid ELL, including granule cell response properties and a slow decay in parallel fiber synaptic strength (Mejias et al., 2013; Lewis and Maler, 2004), which can be considered a form of regularization.
evidence: The claim is supported by two citations (Mejias et al., 2013; Lewis and Maler, 2004).

claim: Adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) shows various patterns of generalization and specificity when training and testing are carried out at different head rotation frequencies or static head tilts.
source: Adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) shows various patterns of generalization and specificity when training and testing are carried out at different head rotation frequencies or static head tilts (Boyden et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Boyden et al., 2004.

claim: Under some experimental conditions, VOR learning has been shown to be quite specific to the training context.
source: Under some experimental conditions, VOR learning has been shown to be quite specific to the training context (Baker et al., 1987; Yakushin et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by two citations (Baker et al., 1987; Yakushin et al., 2000).

claim: Generalization of VOR learning is observed when training at a high head rotation frequency and testing on a lower frequency.
source: Generalization of VOR learning is also observed under some circumstances, for example when training at a high head rotation frequency and testing on a lower frequency (Boyden et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Boyden et al., 2004.

claim: Patterns of generalization in human motor learning can be explained by the tuning of a set of basis elements.
source: It has been suggested that patterns of generalization in human motor learning, such as adaptation to force fields in reaching, can be explained by the tuning of a set of basis elements (Donchin et al., 2003; Ghahramani et al., 1996; Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by three citations (Donchin et al., 2003; Ghahramani et al., 1996; Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994).

claim: The present study is the first to directly relate responses of granule cells recorded during a learning task to generalization.
source: To our knowledge, the present study is the first to directly relate responses of granule cells recorded during a learning task to generalization.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the present study.

claim: All experiments performed in this study adhere to the American Physiological Society's Guiding Principles in the Care and Use of Animals and were approved by the Columbia University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee, protocol AAAW4462.
source: All experiments performed in this study adhere to the American Physiological Society's Guiding Principles in the Care and Use of Animals and were approved by the Columbia University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee, protocol AAAW4462.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance of the research.

claim: Mormyrid fish of the species Gnathonemus petersii (7-12 cm in length) were used in these experiments.
source: Mormyrid fish (7-12 cm in length) of the species Gnathonemus petersii were used in these experiments.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Paralysis blocks the effect of electromotoneurons on the electric organ, preventing the EOD, but the motor command signal that would normally elicit an EOD continues to be emitted spontaneously at rates of 2-5 Hz.
source: Paralysis blocks the effect of electromotoneurons on the electric organ, preventing the EOD, but the motor command signal that would normally elicit an EOD continues to be emitted spontaneously at rates of 2-5 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the effects of the experimental preparation.

claim: Microstimulation-evoked corollary discharge responses were indistinguishable from those evoked by the fish's spontaneous commands at the level of field potentials, mossy fibers, and granule cells.
source: Finally, microstimulation-evoked corollary discharge responses were indistinguishable from those evoked by the fish's spontaneous commands at the level of field potentials, mossy fibers, and granule cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental validation of the microstimulation method.

claim: Ampullary afferents were characterized by highly regular spontaneous firing at ~50 Hz, the absence of any response to the EOD motor command, an excitatory responses to a stomach negative EOD mimic pulse, and strong responses to small, long duration electrosensory stimuli.
source: Consistent with previous studies, ampullary afferents were encountered in the deeper layers of ELL (medial in our penetrations) and were characterized by highly regular spontaneous firing at ~50 Hz, the absence of any response to the EOD motor command, an excitatory responses to a stomach negative EOD mimic pulse (0.2-2 ms duration), and strong responses to small (<1 μA), long duration (10-100 ms) electrosensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a description of the characteristics used to identify ampullary afferents, consistent with previous studies.

claim: E-cells showed increased firing in responses to a stomach negative EOD mimic pulse, while I-cells showed decreased firing.
source: E-cells showed increased firing in responses to a stomach negative EOD mimic pulse, while I-cells showed decreased firing.
evidence: This is a description of the response characteristics used to classify E and I cells.

claim: None of the E- or I-cells included in the analysis exhibited two distinct action potential waveforms, the hallmark of medium ganglion cells.
source: None of the E- or I-cells included in our analysis exhibited two distinct action potential waveforms, the hallmark of the other major cell type of in VLZ, the medium ganglion cells (Bell et al., 1997a; Bell et al., 1993).
evidence: This is a description of the criteria used to exclude medium ganglion cells from the analysis, with citations to Bell et al., 1997a and Bell et al., 1993.
